manuscript_title: From read-out geometry to in-silico stimulation: a distributed

required_revisions.text: Replace the abstract's flagship personalisation claim with the leakage-free number. Promote the population-average LDA-resonant site result (~78% net cure, site chosen entirely from training patients with no per-test-patient search) to the primary headline in title framing, abstract and Results. Report the per-patient 121-way argmax result alongside it and label it explicitly as an upper bound on achievable personalisation at every occurrence, including the abstract. This is the change the panel's two dissenting reviewers converged on and it is the gating item for this decision.

Add the chance-overlap permutation test for Fig. 6 (10,000 draws of random subsets of sizes 35 and 33 from the 121 parcels), report the empirical p-value in the Methods and figure caption, and revise the Fig. 6 title and the corresponding Discussion sentence to match the test outcome. If the observed overlap is not significantly below chance, the disjointness claim must be softened to descriptive language.

Add the reservoir-hyperparameter sensitivity analysis promised in the rebuttal (N \u2208 {1000, 2000, 4000}; spectral radius \u2208 {0.85, 0.95, 0.99}), re-running the \u0394W-based pathology-site ranking and LDA-resonant site selection, and report whether (a) the cortical/subcortical anatomical dissociation and (b) the focal-fails / distributed-succeeds asymmetry are preserved. State plainly in the Results or Discussion whether the dissociation survives; if it does not survive across configurations, scope the claim accordingly. This item is required because the authors' rebuttal to the 'model geometry vs. disease property' critique rests on it.

Rescope causal and translational language throughout title, abstract and the opening of Results, replacing unqualified 'stimulation', 'cure' and 'prescribes how to stimulate' with 'in-silico perturbation' / 'model-prescribed correction' as proposed, and move the existing Discussion caveat (that the reservoir is fit to infraslow BOLD and an intervention here is an abstract input to regional FC dynamics) forward to immediately precede Fig. 4. Also state explicitly that the resonant frequency f_eig derives from the spectrum of J rather than from patient data.

Close the three HARD methods gaps: (a) state the random seed(s) or seed-averaging procedure used to generate J and J_in, and confirm reproducibility of the fixed reservoir; (b) give exact versions for Python, NumPy, scikit-learn, nilearn and Matplotlib, and deposit an environment file or requirements.txt in the GitHub repository; (c) add a participant demographics table (age, sex, education, MMSE or equivalent, and disease-stage information) for both the 40/40 analysis cohorts and the 145/41 full pool, together with the diagnostic and exclusion criteria used to define CC and AD groups (citing or summarising the ADNI protocol).

Add bootstrap 95% confidence intervals (patient-level resampling, 2000 iterations) for AUROC and balanced accuracy in Fig. 3A\u2013D and for the tangent-space SVM benchmark, reported in figure legends and a supplementary table. Also report fit quality (residuals or CIs) for the learning-curve extrapolation in Fig. S1, or explicitly label the projected N=100\u2013200 accuracies as an unvalidated extrapolation.

Define 'physiological amplitude' numerically (the proposed RMS_pert/RMS_base \u2264 2 threshold matching Fig. S10A) in Methods, and state the threshold explicitly at each point in Results where 'physiological' or 'supra-physiological' amplitude is invoked, so that the claim that focal targeting fails 'at any amplitude' is checkable.

Add the missing citations: Luppi et al. (2026, eNeuro) and Bonn\u00ec et al. (2026, Alzheimer's Research & Therapy) in the Discussion, with an explicit contrast of scope and method against the present work; and a standard Riemannian/tangent-space FC classification reference (e.g. Barachant et al.) in the Methods description of the tangent-space SVM benchmark.

Resolve the three citation queries raised by the audit: confirm or correct Ref [6] (Fox et al. 2014, PNAS 111:E4367\u2013E4375, which could not be located and is load-bearing for the focal-target premise); confirm the year and venue of Ref [22] (Koch et al., precuneus rTMS \u2014 the audit located a 2025 Alzheimer's Research & Therapy paper rather than a 2022 Brain paper); and confirm Ref [30] (Vogel et al. 2020, Nat Commun 11:2612). Provide DOIs for all three.

Add the clarity fixes conceded in the rebuttal: (a) a paragraph at the start of the 'In-silico stimulation' Results subsection contrasting read-out interpolation (\u03b1) with input oscillation amplitude (A) before Fig. 4; (b) 2\u20133 sentences in Results defining transductive embedding versus leave-one-patient-out reconstruction in plain language, stating the 17.5%\u219242.5% baseline misclassification shift and its cause at first mention. On the transductive-embedding question specifically, I accept the authors' rebuttal that basis construction across all patients with fold-disjoint classifier training is defensible; no methodological change is required, but the exposition must make the distinction from site-search leakage explicit.

minor_suggestions: Specify a numerical value for the membrane time constant \u03c4 rather than describing it qualitatively as 'effectively instantaneous', and briefly justify the feedback gain f=0.1.
Detail the exact construction of the train-only tangent reference mean in the nested CV (inner vs. outer loop), so the SVM benchmark can be reproduced precisely.
State the ADNI data freeze / release version and download date so readers can assemble the identical cohort.
Add a specific commit hash or release tag to the code-availability statement, and confirm in the repository README that the leave-one-AD-patient-out leakage-free analysis is included.

Specify the reproducibility details conceded in the rebuttal: that the closed-loop reservoir state is inherited from the teacher-forced warmup rather than reset to zero, and that the sinusoid is added to rather than substituted for u(t)=f\u00b7\u015d(t).
Briefly justify N_PC=50 specifically (Fig. S2 shows a plateau at K_PC\u2265100), or note that results are insensitive across that range.
Report hardware and approximate compute time for the main analyses.

Consider a brief note on why 40 CC / 40 AD were chosen for the main analyses given the larger available pool (145/41); a sentence of rationale would pre-empt the reviewers' sample-size question even absent a formal power calculation.
Consider adding a conflict-of-interest statement (even a nil declaration) alongside the existing funding disclosure.

weaknesses.text: {HARD} The two intervention protocols—read-out interpolation (α parameter, Figs. 4–5) and oscillatory stimulation (amplitude A, Figs. 5–7)—are introduced without clear upfront distinction. The text states 'α is distinct from the oscillation amplitude A below' (Methods, p. 22) but this appears only after results are presented. A reader encountering Fig. 4 does not immediately know whether the perturbation is a theoretical read-out edit or a physical drive. Suggest: clarify in the main-text Results section before Fig. 4 that two protocols are being compared and what each represents.

{HARD} The transductive vs. leave-one-out cross-validation distinction is critical to the leakage-free claim but is relegated to Methods (p. 23, 'Leakage-free target selection') and Fig. S9. The main text (p. 12) states 'Honest cross-validation does raise the baseline...' without first explaining what 'honest' means or why the transductive embedding used throughout Figs. 3–5 is not honest. A reader unfamiliar with transductive learning may not grasp why Fig. S9 is necessary or what it changes. Suggest: briefly define transductive vs. leave-one-out in Results before presenting the main stimulation findings, or move the leakage-free analysis to the main text.

{HARD} The term 'physiological amplitude' is used repeatedly (Figs. 4C, 5, Methods p. 22) but is never formally defined in the main text. The Methods state 'supra-physiological amplitude limits' and reference 'fig. S10' for 'physiological diagnostics', but S10 defines it only as 'RMSpert/RMSbase > 1'. What is the threshold for 'physiological'? Is it RMSpert/RMSbase ≤ 2, ≤ 1, or something else? This ambiguity undermines the claim that focal strategies fail 'at any amplitude' (p. 9). Suggest: define the physiological amplitude threshold explicitly in Results or Methods.

{SOFT} The term 'read-out' is used in three distinct senses: (1) the linear decoder W, (2) the output y = W⊤x, and (3) the feature space derived from W (G-space). While context usually disambiguates, the first mention of 'read-out geometry' (p. 5) could be clearer. Suggest: use 'read-out weights' for W, 'read-out output' for y, and 'read-out geometry' for the feature space, or define each sense at first use.

{SOFT} The abstract claims the model 'reconstruct[s] each individual's lagged FC' but does not define 'lagged FC' until Methods (p. 21). For readers unfamiliar with this term, the abstract's claim is opaque. Suggest: either define 'lagged FC' in the abstract or replace with 'temporal structure of connectivity'.

{SOFT} Figure 2I caption states 'median ± IQR' but the plot shows error bars that appear symmetric; IQR is typically asymmetric around the median. Are these actually SD or SEM? The caption should match the plot. Suggest: clarify whether the bands represent IQR or SD/SEM.

{SOFT} The phrase 'a distributed change in the model's connectivity kernel' (abstract, p. 1) is never formally defined. What is the 'connectivity kernel'? Is it the read-out W, the recurrent weights J, or something else? The term appears again in Results (p. 9) but without definition. Suggest: define 'connectivity kernel' at first use or replace with a more standard term.

{SOFT} Quantitative comparisons sometimes lack explicit baselines: e.g., 'modest accuracy, below that of structural atrophy' (abstract) is vague—how much below? The text later states structural AUROC ≈ 0.84 vs. functional ≈ 0.66–0.70 (Supplementary Note S1), but this comparison is relegated to supplementary material. Suggest: state the comparison explicitly in the main text or abstract.

questions: What is the formal definition of 'physiological amplitude' used to evaluate whether focal stimulation fails? Is the threshold RMSpert/RMSbase ≤ 2 (as suggested by Fig. S10A), and does this apply uniformly across all focal protocols?

In the transductive embedding (Figs. 3–5), the SVD basis and LDA discriminant are fit on all patients, then classifiers are evaluated on held-out folds. Does this mean the embedding itself is not held-out, only the classifier? If so, how does this differ from a standard train-test split, and why is it not considered a form of leakage?

The term 'connectivity kernel' in the abstract and Results—does this refer to the read-out weights W, the recurrent weights J, or the effective input-to-output transfer function? A formal definition would clarify the mechanistic claim.

Figure 2I shows agreement between empirical and simulated lagged FC across delays. Does the model's lagged-FC structure emerge from the closed-loop dynamics, or is it inherited from the teacher-forced training? How sensitive is this to the choice of feedback gain f = 0.1?

In Fig. 5A, the theoretical W correction (top-1 column) is 'essentially inert' at α = 50, yet Fig. S5B shows it reaches ~90% reclassification at α = 2. Why does the main text emphasize the inertness at α = 50 rather than the efficacy at α = 2? Is α = 50 chosen as a fair upper bound, or is there a reason to dismiss over-correction?

The LDA-resonant site is selected per patient as the argmax of FC-lag score reduction over 121 sites. In the leave-one-out cross-validation (Fig. S9), is this argmax computed on the training patients only, or is each held-out patient's best site chosen from the training set? The Methods state 'each patient's personalised site chosen as the argmax of the train-only score reduction over the 121 sites'—does this mean the argmax is over 121 sites in the training set, or 121 sites in the full atlas?

weaknesses.text: No confidence intervals reported on the primary classification metrics (AUROC, balanced accuracy) across folds; only mean±SD is given. A 95% CI on AUROC for each classifier would strengthen claims about the modest but above-chance performance and its comparison to the tangent-space benchmark.

The tangent-space SVM benchmark (AUROC 0.75±0.12) is reported as mean±SD over nested CV, but the definition of 'SD' is ambiguous—is this the SD of fold-level AUROCs, or a pooled estimate? The out-of-fold ROC (Fig. 3E) shows AUC≈0.71, which sits at the lower end of the reported range, raising a question about how the mean and SD are computed.

In Fig. 3A–D, the 'reference noise σ' and 'reference K' are chosen by 'marginal-mean AUROC across classifiers,' but it is unclear whether this selection was made on the training set only or involved the test set in any way. If the reference slices were chosen post-hoc to maximise performance, this could introduce a soft bias.

The learning-curve extrapolation (Fig. S1) fits a saturating power law m(N) = A − B·N^(−C) to leave-one-patient-out data, but no confidence band or uncertainty quantification is provided for the projected AUROC at N=100 and N=200. The 68% band shown is from the fit covariance, but the extrapolation range is large and the fit quality is not reported (R², residual plot).

Effect sizes (e.g., the dissociation between pathology sites and therapy sites) are reported qualitatively (e.g., 'only 11 sites shared, ~31% and ~33% of each set'; Fig. 6C) but not with a formal overlap metric or Jaccard index, making the magnitude of the dissociation harder to quantify.

The per-patient amplitude×frequency stimulation landscape (Fig. S8) shows individual and population-level heatmaps, but no summary statistic (e.g., median or IQR of the amplitude needed to cross the decision boundary at resonance) is provided across the 40 patients, limiting reproducibility and generalisability assessment.

In the oscillatory stimulation analysis (Methods, 'Oscillatory stimulation'), the choice of frequency sweep range [0, 0.5] cycles/step is not justified, and it is unclear whether this range was chosen a priori or post-hoc based on preliminary results.

The 'net cure' metric in Fig. S9 (fraction of AD-side patients moved to CC side by stimulation) is a sensible leakage-free measure, but the baseline misclassification rate (42.5% under LOPO) is substantially higher than the transductive baseline (17.5%), making the comparison between transductive and LOPO results harder to interpret without a clearer statement of what is being held constant.

No multiple-comparison correction is applied across the 121 sites tested in the per-site stimulation analysis (Fig. S6A, where 'almost every site is therapeutic on average'). Although the authors note that 120/121 sites move the score toward CC, no Bonferroni or FDR correction is mentioned, and it is unclear whether this is a single exploratory analysis or a hypothesis test.

questions: In Fig. 3, the 'reference slices' for K and σ are chosen by 'marginal-mean AUROC across classifiers'—was this selection made on the training set only, or did it involve any inspection of test-set performance? If the latter, this could introduce selection bias.

The tangent-space SVM benchmark reports AUROC 0.75±0.12 as 'mean±SD over a nested 5×5 patient-level CV.' Can you clarify whether this SD is the standard deviation of the 25 fold-level AUROCs, or a pooled estimate? The out-of-fold ROC (Fig. 3E) shows AUC≈0.71, which is at the lower end of the range; how do these relate?

In Fig. S1, the learning-curve fit m(N) = A − B·N^(−C) is extrapolated to N=100 and N=200. What is the R² of this fit, and how sensitive are the projected AUROC values to the choice of functional form (e.g., would a different saturating model yield substantially different projections)?

For the oscillatory stimulation analysis, was the frequency sweep range [0, 0.5] cycles/step chosen a priori, or was it selected based on preliminary inspection of the data? If the latter, a sensitivity analysis over a wider range would strengthen the claim that f_eig is the true optimum.

In Fig. S6A, you report that 120/121 sites are therapeutic on average at f_1 (A=4). Given that 121 sites are tested, should a multiple-comparison correction (e.g., Bonferroni) be applied to determine which sites are significantly therapeutic? Or is this an exploratory, non-inferential analysis?

The 'net cure' metric in Fig. S9 compares transductive (baseline 17.5% misclassification) and LOPO (baseline 42.5% misclassification) schemes. Can you provide a side-by-side comparison of the stimulation effect (absolute reclassification rate) under both schemes, to clarify whether the LOPO result is genuinely comparable or reflects a different operating point?

In the Methods section ('Leakage-free target selection'), you state that the personalised per-patient LDA-resonant site is 'an upper bound on achievable personalisation.' Can you quantify this bound—e.g., how much of the 100% net cure under LOPO personalisation is due to the per-patient argmax over 121 sites, versus how much would be achieved by a fixed global site?

For the read-out interpolation analysis (Figs. 4, S10), the interpolation strength α is allowed to exceed 1 (α > 1 = over-correction). What is the justification for exploring α > 1, and does the closed-loop dynamics guarantee that α=1 (full replacement by the CC-mean read-out) is insufficient, or is this an empirical observation? A sensitivity analysis showing the effect of capping α at 1 would clarify this.

weaknesses.text: SOFT: The Ethics section could explicitly state that this work is a secondary analysis and therefore exempt from new IRB review, to preempt any ambiguity about whether new approval was sought or required. The current phrasing ('This work is a secondary analysis of de-identified, publicly available human imaging data obtained from ADNI') is correct but does not explicitly invoke exemption language.

SOFT: The manuscript does not acknowledge the use of any AI tools or large language models in analysis, manuscript preparation, or figure generation. Given the computational nature and the date (2026), a statement on AI use (if any) would strengthen transparency, even if none was used.

questions: Was this work reviewed and approved as exempt by the authors' institutional IRB, or did it proceed without new review on the grounds that it is secondary analysis of de-identified public data? An explicit statement of the exemption determination would clarify the compliance pathway.

Were any AI tools, machine-learning models, or large language models used in the analysis pipeline, figure generation, or manuscript preparation? A brief disclosure would be consistent with emerging transparency norms.

The ADNI Data Use Agreement restricts redistribution of raw and derived data. Does the authors' GitHub repository contain any derived imaging data (e.g., preprocessed BOLD time series, FC matrices, or model outputs), or only analysis code and non-data outputs? If derived data are posted, is that consistent with the DUA?

Table S1 lists cohort sizes for each analysis. Are all cohort definitions and exclusion criteria (e.g., the '>100-volume filter' mentioned for the tangent-space SVM benchmark) documented in the Methods or Supplementary Materials, to support reproducibility and audit of data governance?

weaknesses.text: Braak staging attribution unclear: The manuscript states regions 'overlap with regions harbouring early neurofibrillary pathology in Braak staging' (Discussion, p. 16) citing refs. 27–28, but does not specify which regions in the current parcellation correspond to Braak stages I–II or explicitly map subcortical/limbic structures (pallidum, accumbens, brainstem, amygdala) to early Braak stages; the claim is plausible but attribution should be more precise.

Missing directly competing recent work on personalized neuromodulation targeting in AD: The manuscript does not cite Luppi et al. (2026, eNeuro) on connectome-guided personalization of optimal tDCS intervention selection in Alzheimer's disease, which is a directly parallel study using connectome-based models to identify personalized stimulation targets in AD.

Missing Bonnì et al. (2026, Alzheimer's Research & Therapy) on personalized combined magnetic/electrical stimulation of the DMN in mild AD, which is a clinical trial protocol directly relevant to the translational claims in the Discussion; this omission weakens the novelty claim and positioning against concurrent work.

Koch et al. (2022) citation may be outdated: Reference 22 cites the 2022 Brain publication, but a 2025 follow-up exists (Koch et al., Alzheimer's Research & Therapy, 2025) reporting longer-term effects of 52 weeks of precuneus rTMS; clarification is needed on whether 2022 is the initial trial and 2025 is follow-up, or if 2025 supersedes the 2022 report.

Limited coverage of recent in-silico perturbation work: The manuscript cites Spiegler et al. (2016), Muldoon et al. (2016), Kunze et al. (2016), and Deco et al. (2019) on connectome-based stimulation modeling, but more recent work on digital twin brain models and in-silico perturbation (e.g., 2025 publications on personalized long-term recovery and precision non-invasive brain stimulation) exists and should be cited.

Infraslow oscillation literature attribution unclear: The citation of DiAntonio et al. (2026, ref. 20) as a reference for infraslow connectivity is unusual—that paper is about 'Linearizing and forecasting: A reservoir computing route to digital twins of the brain' and may not be the primary source for infraslow oscillation evidence; Fox & Raichle (2007) or Cordes et al. (2001) may be more direct.

Riemannian/tangent-space FC classifier benchmark uncited: The manuscript uses a tangent-space SVM classifier (Fig. 3E, Methods) as a leakage-free baseline but does not cite prior work on Riemannian geometry for FC classification, which is a standard method that should be cited for reproducibility and positioning.

Transductive vs. inductive embedding not discussed in related work: The manuscript acknowledges (Discussion, p. 18) that the embedding is 'transductive' (built across all patients), but the related-work section does not discuss trade-offs between transductive and inductive embeddings in personalized models, which would strengthen the framing.

questions: Can you cite the specific Braak stage mapping for the subcortical/limbic structures (pallidum, accumbens, brainstem, amygdala) identified as most-affected in Fig. 6A? The current citation (refs. 27–28) does not explicitly link these parcels to early Braak stages in the text.

Are you aware of the concurrent connectome-guided personalization work by Luppi et al. (eNeuro, 2026) and the clinical trial protocol by Bonnì et al. (Alzheimer's Research & Therapy, 2026)? If so, how does your work differ in scope or method? If not, these should be cited in revision as directly relevant concurrent work.

Is the 2022 Koch et al. citation the initial trial report, with the 2025 follow-up being a longer-term outcome? Please clarify the relationship and consider citing the 2025 publication if it is the more complete report.

The tangent-space SVM benchmark (Fig. 3E) is a standard method but lacks a citation. Can you provide a reference for the Riemannian geometry approach to FC classification, or confirm that this is a standard application of existing methods?

Is DiAntonio et al. (ref. 20) the appropriate citation for the claim that resting-state connectivity fluctuates in the infraslow band, or would Fox & Raichle (2007) or Cordes et al. (2001) be more direct? The DiAntonio paper appears to be about reservoir computing and digital twins rather than infraslow oscillations per se.

weaknesses.text: HARD: The classifier is trained and tested on the same cohort (transductive embedding, Methods p. 21), and the therapy-target selection criterion is defined by its effect on that same discriminant. This creates a closed loop: the sites that 'cure' the patient are those that move the patient's score toward the CC distribution as defined by the training set. The leave-one-AD-patient-out cross-validation (Fig. S9) rebuilds the discriminant per fold, but the therapy-target selection still uses a per-patient argmax over 121 sites, each scored against the train-only threshold. This is not a fully independent validation—the personalised targets are still selected post-hoc to maximize effect on the discriminant, which is a form of overfitting to the classification objective. The manuscript acknowledges this as an 'upper bound' (Methods, p. 23), but the distinction between the personalised and population-average targets in Fig. S9 is not clearly explained in the main text, leaving ambiguity about which result is the honest one.

HARD: The model is fit to each subject's own data (Methods, Eq. 2), and the perturbation analysis (Figs. 4–5) modifies the read-out W or its input, then re-scores the same model on the same data (teacher-forced FC-lag features). This is not a true out-of-sample validation of the therapy effect. The closed-loop free-run (Fig. 5) is a step toward independence, but it still uses the same fitted model and the same subject's data. There is no held-out test set or independent cohort to verify that the therapy sites identified in one patient generalize to another, or that the dissociation between pathology and therapy sites is not an artifact of the model's fitting procedure.

HARD: The 'stimulation' is an abstract modification of the read-out W or its input, not a literal physical protocol. The mapping between in-silico amplitude (α or A) and a deliverable dose is 'approximate' (Discussion, p. 18), and the optimal frequency (f_eig ≈ 0.026 Hz) is derived from the BOLD-based model, not from electrophysiology or any independent measure of brain dynamics. The claim that 'the model prescribes where and how to stimulate' (Abstract, p. 1; Discussion, p. 17) overstates the translational validity of the prescription. The model is phenomenological and fit to infraslow BOLD correlations; it does not capture cellular mechanisms, neuromodulatory systems, or the actual biophysics of stimulation. The authors acknowledge this ('the reservoir is fit to infraslow BOLD connectivity, not electrophysiology', Discussion, p. 18), but the framing in the abstract and introduction suggests a more direct path to intervention than the evidence supports.

SOFT: The choice of reservoir architecture (fixed random recurrent weights, linear read-out, N=2000 units, spectral radius 0.95, τ ≈ 0, σ_in = 0.01) is not justified or ablated. Why these specific hyperparameters? How sensitive are the results to changes in N, spectral radius, or τ? The read-out regularisation σ is swept (Fig. 3C,D), but the reservoir itself is not. This is a potential confound: the dissociation between pathology and therapy sites might depend on the reservoir's representational geometry, which is fixed by these choices. A sensitivity analysis or ablation would strengthen the claim that the dissociation is a property of the network, not the model.

SOFT: The comparison to the tangent-space SVM benchmark (Fig. 3E, AUROC 0.75±0.12) is fair, but it uses a different preprocessing (global signal regression, 557 CC + 145 AD sessions) and a different cross-validation scheme (nested 5×5 subject-grouped, train-only tangent reference) than the main analysis (40 CC + 40 AD subjects, transductive embedding). The two are not directly comparable on the same data/splits, making it hard to assess whether the reservoir-based read-outs are truly at the 'lower end' of the benchmark's spread or whether the difference is methodological.

SOFT: The empirical lagged FC (143 CC, 40 AD; Fig. 3, text p. 6) is classified at AUROC ≈ 0.71, comparable to the model-based FC-lag (AUROC ≈ 0.70). This is presented as evidence that the model 'repackages the same signal', but the sample sizes differ (143 vs 40 CC), and the comparison is not on identical data/splits. If the empirical lagged FC is equally informative, why use the model at all for classification? The answer (stimulation acts on dynamics, not tissue loss) is valid, but the comparison should be on matched data to support the claim that the model adds no diagnostic information.

SOFT: The selection of the 'most-affected' sites by ||ΔW|| is acknowledged as problematic (Discussion, p. 16: 'these are also among the most weakly inter-connected nodes of the parcellation, where the per-subject read-out is least constrained'). This is a confound: the sites with the largest ||ΔW|| may be those where the read-out is most poorly estimated, not those where pathology is greatest. The authors note this caveat, but it undermines the interpretation of Fig. 6A,B as a map of pathology, and raises the question: are the therapy sites (Fig. 6D) effective because they are well-connected hubs, or because they are the sites where the model's read-out is most constrained and hence most responsive to perturbation?

SOFT: The oscillatory stimulation protocol (Methods, p. 22) uses the leading eigenmode frequency f_eig of the fixed reservoir J, which is a property of the model, not the subject. This is not subject-specific, yet the therapy-target selection (LDA-resonant) is highly personalised (33 distinct sites for 40 patients, Fig. 6D). The interaction between site and frequency is explored (Fig. S6), but it is unclear whether the personalised sites are effective because they are individually optimal or because they are cortical hubs that couple well to the dominant mode regardless of subject. A per-subject frequency optimization would test this.

SOFT: The manuscript claims the AD signature is 'functionally irreducible' to focal sites (Introduction, p. 2; Discussion, p. 15), but the evidence is that focal sites fail to revert the classification at physiological amplitudes. This is consistent with a distributed signature, but it does not rule out the possibility that a multi-site distributed intervention (e.g., simultaneous stimulation of 5–10 sites) could be more efficient than a single site. The full-W correction (Fig. 4B,E) succeeds, but it is not a realistic intervention; the paper does not explore whether a sparse, multi-site pattern could achieve similar efficacy at lower total dose.

questions: In Fig. S9, the 'personalised LDA-resonant' result (100% net cure) uses a per-patient argmax over 121 sites. Is this a true out-of-sample prediction, or is it overfitting to the held-out patient's own data? If the latter, what is the honest, fully independent estimate of the therapy effect?

The reservoir hyperparameters (N, spectral radius, τ, σ_in) are fixed across all subjects. How sensitive are the pathology/therapy dissociation and the classification accuracy to these choices? Has an ablation or sensitivity analysis been performed?

The 'most-affected' sites (Fig. 6A,B) are ranked by ||ΔW||, but the authors note these are weakly inter-connected nodes where the read-out is least constrained. Could the large ||ΔW|| reflect poor estimation rather than pathology? How would you distinguish these?

The empirical lagged FC (AUROC ≈ 0.71) is as informative as the model-based FC-lag (AUROC ≈ 0.70). Why not use the empirical lagged FC directly for the stimulation analysis, rather than fitting a model? Does the model add any diagnostic or mechanistic insight beyond repackaging the same signal?

The optimal driving frequency (f_eig ≈ 0.026 Hz) is derived from the BOLD-based model. Is there any independent evidence (e.g., from electrophysiology, animal models, or prior human studies) that this frequency is biologically relevant for AD or neuromodulation?

The therapy-target selection criterion (LDA-resonant) is defined by its effect on the disease discriminant. Is there a risk that this criterion simply selects sites that are most effective at moving the score, regardless of whether they restore healthy connectivity or merely shift the FC-lag features toward the CC distribution? Could the 'cure' be a statistical artifact rather than a biological restoration?

In Fig. 5, the personalised LDA-resonant site achieves 100% reclassification at supra-physiological amplitude (A ≈ 6), whereas the population-average site reaches only ≈65%. How much of this difference is due to personalisation per se, versus overfitting to the training cohort? What would the per-patient effect be under true leave-one-patient-out cross-validation of the site selection?

The manuscript states that 'no single anatomical landmark serves all individuals' (Discussion, p. 17), yet the population-average LDA-resonant site (left Default-network prefrontal cortex, Fig. S3A) is effective for ≈65% of patients (Fig. S9B). Is this sufficient to justify a one-size-fits-all intervention, or is personalisation truly necessary?

The closed-loop controller (Fig. 5D–F) uses a sliding-window estimate of the FC-lag biomarker. How is this window chosen (length, update frequency)? How sensitive is the closed-loop efficacy to these parameters?

Could the dissociation between pathology sites (subcortical/limbic) and therapy sites (cortical) reflect the structure of the parcellation or the connectivity of the atlas, rather than a genuine property of the AD network? For example, if cortical hubs are more densely connected, they may be more effective at propagating perturbations, regardless of where pathology originates.

weaknesses.text: Circular logic in discriminant-aligned targeting: LDA-resonant site is selected because its resonant drive moves FC-lag score toward control distribution—it succeeds by construction on the same discriminant used for diagnosis, not because it identifies an independent property of therapeutic responsiveness.

Transductive embedding and per-subject read-out fitting: FC-lag and G-space embeddings built transductively across all patients (including test patients) before classifiers trained on disjoint folds; while classifiers are cross-validated, feature space itself is not blind to test set, potentially inflating apparent stability or generalizability.

Supra-physiological amplitudes required for reclassification: successful discriminant-aligned single-site resonant drive requires A ≈ 6–7 (RMS_pert/RMS_base ≈ 6–7), far beyond endogenous drive amplitude; closed-loop reduces to A ≈ 3.3 (~3× baseline), still not clearly physiological.

Modest sample size and cross-sectional design: main cohort is 36 CC and 40 AD subjects (one session each); learning-curve analysis projects AUROC ≈0.76 at N=100 and ≈0.80 at N=200, indicating present accuracy is sample-size-limited; cross-sectional design means disease signature based on group differences, not longitudinal tracking.

Phenomenological rather than biophysical model: reservoir is fixed random recurrent network with linear read-out, not biophysically grounded; stimulation is idealized modification, not literal physical protocol; infraslow frequency (0.026 Hz) appropriate for BOLD but may not translate to electrophysiological or optogenetic protocols.

Limited systematic comparison to prior work on distributed vs. focal AD signatures: claim that 'whether its FC signature reduces to a few focal sites has not been tested causally' (Abstract) is strong but not fully supported by systematic literature review; prior work on Braak staging and network diffusion models of tau spread not deeply engaged.

Heterogeneity of per-patient therapy sites not validated: 33 distinct sites selected across 40 AD patients (each site selected by ≤3 patients); heterogeneity presented as evidence for personalized targeting, but stability under perturbations (resampling, noise injection, parameter variation) not reported, leaving unclear whether this reflects genuine biological variability vs. model noise.

Limited engagement with network-medicine mechanism: authors invoke principle that optimal target is network node most effectively coupled to symptom circuit, but do not formally test this—no comparison to coupling measures, network centrality, or betweenness; dissociation is documented but mechanistic explanation (cortical hubs propagate corrections) is plausible but not rigorously tested.

Oscillatory stimulation results are secondary and not clearly translatable: infraslow prescription (0.026 Hz) is in different band than gamma (40 Hz) explored in recent AD neuromodulation trials; authors acknowledge 'we make no claim about a specific deliverable protocol' but do not clearly explain why infraslow should be preferred.

questions: Were the G-space and FC-lag results in Figs. 3–6 recomputed under a fully honest (non-transductive) embedding, where the SVD basis is built only on the training set? If not, can you provide this analysis or clarify how much the transductive construction inflates apparent discriminability?

How would you distinguish between (a) the LDA-resonant site being a genuine property of the network's therapeutic responsiveness, and (b) it succeeding simply because it is optimized on the discriminant? Could you propose independent validation—e.g., does the LDA-resonant site generalize to a held-out test set or to a different classifier (e.g., random forest)?

You note that pathology sites are 'among the most weakly inter-connected nodes of the parcellation, where the per-subject read-out is least constrained' (p. 9). Could the ranking of pathology sites be an artifact of regularization or fitting procedure rather than true disease severity? How sensitive is the ranking to choice of regularization noise σ?

Is the per-patient site selection stable under perturbations? For example, if you add small noise to FC-lag features or resample the training set, do selected sites remain the same, or does heterogeneity reflect genuine biological variability vs. model noise?

Is the resonant frequency f_eig ≈ 0.077 cycles/step (0.026 Hz) specific to AD patients or the same for controls? If the same, does this suggest the frequency is a property of the fixed reservoir J rather than a disease-specific feature?

You show full-W correction (all 121 sites) reverts classification while focal corrections fail. How many sites are needed to achieve reclassification? Is there a threshold (e.g., 10, 20, 50 sites) above which correction becomes effective? This would clarify whether the signature is truly distributed or merely requires a small number of coordinated sites.

How does your finding that pathology concentrates in subcortical/limbic regions (pallidum, accumbens, brainstem, amygdala) compare to Braak staging and neuropathological maps of tau and amyloid in AD? Are identified sites consistent with early pathology or do they reflect a different aspect of disease?

weaknesses.text: ADNI data are controlled-access and require registration and data-use agreement acceptance; the manuscript states 'available to qualified researchers upon registration' (Methods, Data and code availability), which is a hard gate for independent replication. While this is a legitimate data-access model, it means a replicator cannot obtain the raw data without institutional approval and ADNI consent, creating friction that must be disclosed.

The transductive embedding construction is ambiguous: the manuscript states 'the SVD embeddings were built transductively (across all patients) while the classifiers were trained and tested on disjoint folds' (Methods, Classification), but it is unclear whether the Gram-matrix SVD for FC-lag features is computed once on all patients and then projected per-fold, or recomputed per fold. This is critical for assessing leakage and reproducibility. The leave-one-patient-out (LOPO) variant is described separately (Methods, Leakage-free target selection), but the default transductive procedure's exact fold-wise operation is not explicit.

The closed-loop reconstruction procedure has an ambiguous reset/initialization step: the manuscript states 'the reservoir was reset and run closed-loop: the real target drove the network for the first 5 steps, after which it free-ran' (Methods, Closed-loop reconstruction), but does not specify how the reservoir state x(t) is initialised (zero, random, or from teacher-forced warmup). This affects reproducibility of the lagged-FC validation (Fig. 2I).

The read-out 'G-space' projection is incompletely specified: the manuscript projects W onto the row space of X using 'the top K_PC=200 right singular vectors of X' (Methods, Read-out G-space), but does not state whether X is computed per-session or pooled across sessions, and whether the SVD is recomputed per fold or shared. The justification (Fig. S2) shows training/test error but does not validate the choice against the classification results.

The population-average LDA-resonant site selection (Fig. S3A, S9B) is described as 'the site whose resonant drive moves that patient's FC-lag discriminant most toward CC' (Methods, Leakage-free target selection), but the exact ranking criterion (argmax of score reduction, or argmax of per-site effect size?) is stated only in the LOPO section and not clearly applied to the transductive case. This affects reproducibility of Fig. 5A and Fig. S3.

Software versions are not provided: the manuscript lists Python libraries (NumPy, scikit-learn, nilearn, Matplotlib) but does not specify versions, scikit-learn hyperparameter defaults (e.g., solver for LDA, tree depth limits for RF), or Python version. This is a SOFT issue but limits exact reproducibility of the classifiers.

The exact order of operations for the oscillatory stimulation is not fully specified: the manuscript states 'a sinusoid A sin(2πft) is injected as additional input at the top-k sites during the teacher-forced pass, with W unchanged' (Methods, Oscillatory stimulation), but does not clarify whether the oscillation is added to the target-driven input u(t)=f·ŝ(t) or injected separately, and whether the reservoir state is reset between frequency/amplitude sweeps.

The feedback gain f=0.1 is stated for teacher-forcing but not justified or swept; it is unclear whether this choice affects the relative amplitude comparisons (e.g., RMS_pert/RMS_base in Fig. S10) or the resonance frequency.

The even/odd test–retest ceiling (Fig. 2I, grey line) is mentioned but not defined: it is unclear whether this is computed from the empirical data (splitting sessions into even/odd volumes) or from the model, and over which sessions/patients the median is taken.

questions: Can you clarify the exact procedure for the transductive SVD embedding in the classification pipeline (Methods, Classification)? Specifically, is the Gram-matrix SVD computed once on all patients and then the resulting coordinates projected per fold, or is it recomputed within each training fold? This is critical for assessing whether test-set information leaks into the embedding.

How is the reservoir state x(t) initialised at the start of the closed-loop reconstruction (Methods, Closed-loop reconstruction)? Is it zero, or does it inherit state from the teacher-forced warmup? This affects reproducibility of Fig. 2I.
In the read-out G-space projection (Methods, Read-out G-space), is the SVD of X computed per-session or pooled across all sessions? Is it recomputed per cross-validation fold?

For the population-average LDA-resonant site selection (Fig. S3A, S9B), what is the exact ranking criterion? Is it argmax of the mean FC-lag score reduction across training patients, or argmax of the mean per-site effect size? How is this applied in the transductive case (Fig. 5A)?
Can you provide the versions of Python, NumPy, scikit-learn, and other key libraries used? This will help ensure exact reproducibility of the classifiers.

In the oscillatory stimulation (Methods, Oscillatory stimulation), is the sinusoid A sin(2πft) added to the teacher-forced input u(t)=f·ŝ(t), or injected as a separate input channel? Is the reservoir state reset between frequency/amplitude sweeps?
The feedback gain f=0.1 is used for teacher-forcing but not justified. Was this parameter swept, and does it affect the relative amplitude comparisons (RMS_pert/RMS_base) or the resonance frequency?
How is the even/odd test–retest ceiling (Fig. 2I, grey line) computed? Is it from the empirical data (splitting into even/odd volumes) or from the model, and over which sessions/patients?

weaknesses.text: **HARD: Title and abstract claim causality without sufficient warrant.** The title states 'a distributed functional-connectivity signature of Alzheimer's disease' and the abstract claims 'the ideal correction that maps a patient's dynamics onto the control template is a distributed change'—but this is an observation about what the fitted model requires, not a causal discovery about the disease itself. The model is fit to cross-sectional data; it does not establish that the disease *is* distributed in the biological sense, only that the model's read-out deviations are distributed. The claim 'whether its FC signature reduces to a few focal sites has not been tested causally' (Introduction) frames the question as causal, but the answer—that the model requires distributed correction—does not settle whether the underlying disease pathology is focal or distributed; it only shows the model's representational geometry. This is a SOFT-to-HARD boundary: the framing invites a causal/biological reading that the evidence does not support.

**HARD: Generalization beyond the fitted model.** The abstract and Results claim 'the site to stimulate is not where the read-out deviation is largest but where the network is most therapeutically responsive' as a general principle. However, this is demonstrated only within the fitted reservoir model on this cohort. Whether this dissociation holds in actual brain tissue, in other models, or in other cohorts is not tested. The claim is presented as a finding about neuromodulation strategy in general ('Optimal targets are cortical and heterogeneous: effective neuromodulation requires model-informed, personalised targeting'), but it is a finding about this model on this data. The Discussion does hedge ('Whether this dissociation reflects the biology of AD or the representational geometry of the model is a question our framework raises but cannot, on its own, settle'), but the abstract and main narrative do not, creating a scope mismatch.

**HARD: Causal language for in-silico perturbations.** The paper uses 'stimulation', 'intervention', 'drive', and 'cure' throughout to describe read-out interpolations and input oscillations applied to a phenomenological model. These are not stimulations in the neurobiological sense; they are mathematical modifications of a fitted linear read-out or inputs to a fixed random reservoir. The closed-loop section (Fig. 5) calls the controller 'adaptive (closed-loop) neuromodulation' and states 'a causally available, minimal-dose perturbation', but causality here is causal availability in the model's information flow, not causal efficacy in the brain. The Discussion acknowledges 'the reservoir is fit to infraslow BOLD connectivity, not electrophysiology, so an "intervention" here is an abstract input to the regional FC dynamics', but the main text and abstract do not carry this caveat, and the language ('reclassified', 'cured', 'therapeutic') implies a real intervention. This is HARD because the causal framing is misleading without the caveat front and center.

**SOFT: Claim about 'complete reclassification' under-hedged.** The abstract states 'selecting each patient's site by its effect on the disease discriminant achieves complete, individualised reclassification from one site'. Figure 5A shows 100% reclassification in the open-loop case, but this is achieved at supra-physiological amplitude (A=6, Fig. S10), and the closed-loop version reaches only 97.5% (39/40, Fig. 5D). The leakage-free version (Fig. S9) reaches ~100% for personalised targets but ~78% for the population-average site. The word 'complete' is accurate for the open-loop transductive case but not for the honest cross-validation, and the amplitude caveat is not in the abstract.

**SOFT: 'Distributed' vs 'not focal' conflation.** The paper argues that because targeting the top-1 or top-5 most-deviant sites fails, the signature is 'distributed'. However, 'distributed' could mean (i) the pathology is spread across many regions, (ii) the discriminative signal requires many regions to read out, or (iii) the therapeutic effect requires many regions to achieve. The evidence shows (ii) and (iii) within the model, but does not distinguish whether the underlying pathology is truly distributed or whether the model's representational geometry simply requires a distributed read-out to capture a focal lesion. The Discussion hints at this ('Whether this dissociation reflects the biology of AD or the representational geometry of the model'), but the main claims treat 'distributed' as a property of the disease, not the model.

**SOFT: Learning-curve extrapolation (Fig. S1) presented without uncertainty bounds on the projection.** The paper extrapolates AUROC to N=100 and N=200 patients per group, projecting ~0.76 and ~0.80 respectively. These are point estimates from a power-law fit; the 68% band shown is the fit uncertainty, not a confidence interval on the extrapolation. The claim 'the modest present accuracy reflects sample size rather than a ceiling of the representation' is reasonable but depends on the extrapolation being accurate, which is not guaranteed. This is SOFT because the caveat is present but the projection is given prominent placement in the main narrative.

**SOFT: Anatomical interpretation of ΔW sites under-hedged.** The paper states 'The siteswiththelargestper-patientcorrectionmagnitude∥ΔW∥wereconsistentlysubcorticalandlimbic,mostfrequentlythe bilateral pallidum and nucleus accumbens, the brainstem and the amygdala', then notes 'these are, however, also among the most weakly inter-connected nodes of the parcellation, where a shared reservoir basis constrains the per-subject read-out least; the ranking should thus be read as indicating where the correction kernel carries its largest weights, not as an independently validated map of Alzheimer pathology.' This caveat is appropriate but buried in the text; the anatomical claim is stated first and prominently (Fig. 6A,B), creating an impression of validated pathology localization that the caveat undermines.

**HARD: Claim that 'pathology sites and therapeutic sites are largely disjoint' (Fig. 6 title) is not tested statistically.** The paper shows 11 of 35 pathology sites and 11 of 33 therapy sites overlap (~31% each), and states 'the great majority of each set is exclusive to that criterion'. However, no statistical test of whether this overlap is less than expected by chance is provided. If the 121 sites were randomly partitioned into two sets of 35 and 33, what overlap would be expected? Without this, the claim of dissociation is qualitative. This is HARD because the headline claim (Fig. 6 title, Discussion) rests on a quantitative comparison that is not formally tested.

questions: The abstract claims the signature is 'distributed' and 'not reducible' to focal sites. Can the authors clarify whether this is a claim about the disease's biological pathology, the model's representational geometry, or both? The Discussion acknowledges the ambiguity, but the abstract does not.

In Fig. 5A, the open-loop LDA-resonant drive achieves 100% reclassification at A=6, but Fig. S10B shows this requires ~44× baseline amplitude at the driven site. How does this amplitude compare to typical non-invasive neuromodulation (e.g., tDCS, TMS) in physical units, and does the paper intend to claim feasibility or only methodological proof-of-concept?

The leakage-free cross-validation (Fig. S9) shows the population-average LDA-resonant site achieves ~78% net cure, not 100%. Should the abstract's claim of 'complete, individualised reclassification' be qualified to reflect the honest cross-validation result, or is the transductive result the intended headline?

The paper argues that the dissociation between pathology sites (ΔW-ranked) and therapy sites (LDA-resonant) is 'expected rather than paradoxical' because they answer different questions. Can the authors provide a formal test (e.g., permutation test, overlap-by-chance calculation) to quantify whether the observed disjointness (Fig. 6C) is statistically significant, or is the visual dissociation sufficient for the claim?

The resonant frequency f_eig ≈ 0.077 cycles/step corresponds to ~0.026 Hz in physical time. The paper notes this is 'in the well-established infraslow band in which resting-state connectivity itself fluctuates', but does not test whether this frequency is specific to AD or is a property of the reservoir's fixed dynamics shared across all subjects. Is the resonance subject-specific or a fixed property of J?

The paper claims the model 'prescribes not only where but how to stimulate' (Discussion), but the frequency prescription is derived from the reservoir's eigenspectrum, not from the AD data. How much of the frequency tuning (Fig. S7A) is driven by the model's intrinsic resonance versus the disease-specific FC-lag signal? Could a different model with different eigenspectrum yield a different optimal frequency?

Figure 3 shows the two read-outs (G-space and FC-lag) reach comparable AUROC (~0.66–0.70) and plateau near K≈25. Is there evidence that these two feature spaces are capturing the same underlying signal, or could they be independent sources of weak discrimination that happen to plateau at similar accuracy?

The paper uses a transductive embedding (SVD across all patients) for classification, then applies leave-one-patient-out cross-validation. Does the transductive embedding introduce leakage in the main results (Figs. 3–5), and should the honest cross-validation (Fig. S9) be the primary reported result rather than a supplementary check?
